nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: High N requirement: typical rate 150–200 lb N/acre for grain production in the Southeast, depending on yield goal and soil organic matter.
nitrogenBehavior.note: Corn is one of the most N-demanding row crops. Residue has moderate C:N ratio (~40–60:1) and decomposes relatively quickly.

residue.description: High stover volume, relatively persistent through winter but decomposes more rapidly than cereal rye straw.

crops.rootSystem: Fibrous, relatively shallow compared with taproot crops.

pollinationSilking.note: Pollination and silking typically occur in July–August in the North Carolina Piedmont. Heat stress above 35 °C and moisture deficits during this window can reduce kernel set.
pollinationSilking.source: NC State Extension Corn Production Guide

growingWindow.description: Full-season corn in the NC Piedmont is typically planted mid-April to early May and harvested September–October.

diseasePestNotes: Corn residue can harbor Fusarium species that may affect subsequent small-grain crops.
Rootworm and cutworm management may be needed in continuous-corn systems.

sources.citation: NC State Extension Corn Production Guide

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Fixes atmospheric N via Bradyrhizobium symbiosis when effectively nodulated. Most fixed N is sequestered in crop biomass and removed with grain harvest.

residualNcredit.note: NC State Extension estimates approximately 15–30 lb N/acre as a residual nitrogen credit following soybean. This is a contextual estimate, not a guaranteed field-specific amount.
residualNcredit.source: NC State Extension Soybean Production Guide

nitrogenBehavior.note: Soybean grain exports substantial nitrogen. Do not treat all biological N fixation as a next-crop fertilizer replacement.

residue.description: Relatively low-residue profile compared with corn or small grains; residue decomposes readily.

podFill.note: Pod fill and seed development typically occur August–September. Moisture stress and prolonged heat can reduce seed size and yield.
podFill.source: NC State Extension Soybean Production Guide

growingWindow.description: Full-season soybean in the NC Piedmont is typically planted May–June and harvested October–November.

diseasePestNotes: Soybean cyst nematode (SCN, Heterodera glycines) can build populations in continuous or frequent soybean rotations.
White mold (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum) risk increases in cool, wet conditions and with tight rotations involving other susceptible hosts.
Moderate non-host break intervals help manage SCN.

sources.citation: NC State Extension Soybean Production Guide

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Moderate N requirement; timing is important (split applications in spring).
nitrogenBehavior.note: Straw residues have high C:N ratio and can contribute to soil organic matter but may temporarily immobilize N if incorporated fresh.

residue.description: Significant straw biomass after grain harvest; provides ground-cover value if left on the surface.

crops.rootSystem: Fibrous root system that develops in fall and resumes growth in spring.

grainFill.note: Grain filling and maturity occur in May–June for winter wheat in the NC Piedmont.
grainFill.source: NC State Extension Small Grain Production Guide

growingWindow.description: Winter wheat is planted in the fall (October–November), winters over, and is harvested the following June in the NC Piedmont.

diseasePestNotes: Fusarium head blight (scab) risk can increase when wheat follows corn or sorghum due to shared Fusarium inoculum in residue.
Hessian fly and rust diseases should be monitored.

sources.citation: NC State Extension Small Grain Production Guide

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Moderate N requirement, generally somewhat less per unit yield than corn.
nitrogenBehavior.note: High-biomass stover residue can contribute organic matter but may carry Fusarium inoculum affecting subsequent small grains.

residue.description: High-biomass stover that can improve soil coverage but decomposes more slowly than corn stover.

crops.rootSystem: Fibrous, deep rooting capacity under drought stress.

grainFill.note: Grain filling typically occurs in August–September. Sorghum is more drought-resilient than corn during this period.

growingWindow.description: Grain sorghum in the NC Piedmont is typically planted May–June and harvested September–October.

diseasePestNotes: Fusarium head blight risk to subsequent wheat should be considered.
Sorghum can host some pests shared with corn.

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Moderate N requirement; deep taproot can scavenge nutrients from lower soil profiles.
nitrogenBehavior.note: Can extract water and nutrients from deeper soil layers due to taproot architecture.

residue.description: Moderate residue from stalks and heads; persistent through winter.

crops.rootSystem: Deep taproot that can extend below the typical corn root zone.

flowering.note: Flowering typically occurs in July–August. Heat stress and moisture deficits can reduce oil content in oil-type varieties.

growingWindow.description: Sunflowers in the NC Piedmont are typically planted May–June and harvested September–October.

diseasePestNotes: Sclerotinia head rot and white mold are concerns; sunflower and soybean can both be hosts associated with Sclerotinia sclerotiorum.
A short rotation interval may not provide an adequate disease break for Sclerotinia. Extension guidance recommends managing field history and variety selection.

sources.citation: NC State Extension Plant Pathology — Sclerotinia

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Nitrogen scavenger. Can temporarily immobilize available nitrogen due to high C:N ratio in residue.
nitrogenBehavior.immobilizationRisk: Rye terminated at late boot or past can have C:N ratios >40:1, temporarily tying up available N in spring. Early termination reduces immobilization risk.
nitrogenBehavior.source: NC State Extension Organic Grains — Cover Crops

residue.description: High biomass and very persistent residue that provides excellent soil coverage and erosion protection.

crops.rootSystem: Dense, fibrous root system that scavenges available nutrients.

growingWindow.description: Winter cover crop planted September–October and terminated mid-March to mid-April in the NC Piedmont.

diseasePestNotes: Generally low disease concerns, but can host some nematodes if grown continuously.
Late termination can reduce spring soil moisture available for the next cash crop.

sources.citation: NC State Extension Organic Grains — Cover Crops

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Legume cover crop that can contribute nitrogen to the following crop.

residualNcredit.note: NC State Extension reports approximately 60–75 lb N/acre following crimson clover. Actual contribution depends on biomass production, maturity at termination, and growing conditions.
residualNcredit.source: NC State Extension Winter Annual Cover Crops

nitrogenBehavior.note: N contribution varies with biomass, maturity, termination timing, and growing conditions. Do not treat as a guaranteed fertilizer replacement.

residue.description: Soft residue that decomposes relatively quickly compared with cereal rye.

crops.rootSystem: Shallow taproot with some nitrogen fixation nodules.

growingWindow.description: Winter legume cover crop planted September–October and terminated in spring before full bloom for maximum N contribution.

diseasePestNotes: Generally low disease pressure; provides break from grass-family diseases.

sources.citation: NC State Extension Winter Annual Cover Crops

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Legume cover crop with high nitrogen-fixation potential.

residualNcredit.note: NC State Extension reports approximately 80–100 lb N/acre following hairy vetch. Actual contribution depends on biomass, maturity, termination timing, and growing conditions.
residualNcredit.source: NC State Extension Winter Annual Cover Crops

nitrogenBehavior.note: Volunteer growth can be an issue if seed is allowed to mature. Termination timing affects both N contribution and volunteer management.

residue.description: Viny residue that provides moderate soil coverage; decomposes faster than cereal rye.

growingWindow.description: Winter legume cover crop planted September–October and typically terminated April–May in the NC Piedmont.

diseasePestNotes: May harbor some pests if not rotated; generally beneficial as a break crop.
Volunteer hairy vetch can become a weed in subsequent crops if allowed to set seed.

sources.citation: NC State Extension Winter Annual Cover Crops

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Nitrogen scavenger; bio-drilling effect from deep taproot can improve compaction layers but does not fix atmospheric N.
nitrogenBehavior.note: Can scavenge residual N from lower soil profiles, making it available to subsequent shallow-rooted crops.

residue.description: Can winter-kill in the NC Piedmont, leaving minimal spring living cover. Tissue decomposes rapidly.

crops.rootSystem: Deep taproot (bio-drill) that can penetrate compacted subsoil layers; typically winter-kills.

growingWindow.description: Planted late summer–early fall; typically winter-kills in the NC Piedmont. Leaves root channels that may improve water infiltration.

diseasePestNotes: Can host clubroot if Brassica diseases are present in the field history.
Winter-kill behavior means less spring erosion protection than living cover crops.

sources.citation: NC State Extension Small Farms — Winter Crops

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Warm-season biomass producer and nutrient scavenger.
nitrogenBehavior.note: Rapid growth in summer heat; can produce significant biomass for grazing or soil coverage.

residue.description: Significant warm-season biomass; stems are moderately persistent.

crops.rootSystem: Fibrous, dense root system that improves soil structure.

growingWindow.description: Summer cover crop planted after small-grain harvest and terminated before fall planting.

diseasePestNotes: Generally resistant to many diseases that affect corn and sorghum.
Provides a beneficial break from grass-family diseases when rotated with corn or sorghum.

sources.citation: NC State Extension Summer Annual Forages

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Nitrogen scavenger; moderate C:N ratio compared with cereal rye.
nitrogenBehavior.note: Less persistent residue than cereal rye; decomposes more readily.

residue.description: Moderate biomass that winter-kills in the NC Piedmont, providing some spring residue cover but less persistent protection than rye.

crops.rootSystem: Fibrous root system that provides some soil stabilization.

growingWindow.description: Winter cover crop that typically winter-kills in the NC Piedmont. Less spring biomass than cereal rye but may allow earlier spring field access.

diseasePestNotes: Generally low disease pressure; can host some cereal diseases at low levels.
Winter-kill means less spring coverage than living cover crops like cereal rye or crimson clover.

sources.citation: NC State Extension Small Farms — Winter Crops
